She said: Mr. Speaker, this proposed amendment to Bill C-28 is to change the date of implementation of the clause from April 26, 1989, to April 26, 1990. This clause is poorly drafted and the fear of leasing companies is that this change will cause many small leasing companies to go out of business, therefore, we should be taking a very careful second look at this clause.
The Income Tax Act amendments on leasing are an attempt by the Department of Finance to close off an area of tax revenue loss. The department feels that some firms are using leasing in preference to outright purchases because the leasing companies can capture some tax advantages that the lessee firms themselves cannot.
The strategy behind the amendments is to treat leasing companies as if they are financing companies making loans and to allow those lessee firms which can claim tax advantages to do so if they want to, but the assets are to be treated as a purchase of the lease asset for tax purposes.
The goal seems to be to make those lessees who were only leasing for tax reasons indifferent between leasing and buying with the purchase being financed by loan, and to put those lessees who were leasing for non-tax reasons in exactly the same financial position as before.
As I said earlier, the clause is poorly drafted primarily because it describes how lessees are to be treated under the new clause only, with the description of how lessors are to be treated under new income tax regulations as opposed to insertion of an entirely new clause into the Income Tax Act which is what clause 7 is.
The culmination of this new clause in the Income Thx Act and the new regulations introduce a fundamental change in the way leasing is viewed by the Department of Finance.
It is rather peculiar to do one-half of the changes through amendments to the Income Thx Act and the other half through amendments to the regulations.
The new regulations introduced a considerable change in the complexity of a leasing agreement. The calculations required are not of themselves difficult, nor do they require any information.
On the other hand, the old system is clearly designed to minimize bookkeeping by allowing aggregation over property classes. The new system does show a different approach by the Department of Finance to the ending of perceived tax abuses. Normally, the Department of Finance rewrites the act or regulations to stop the abuses directly by saying "you cannot". The new system for leasing requires the lessor to compare two options and choose the least favourable.
In the words of the legislative committee's researcher, it is not hard to believe that the conclusion of this computation is not foregone. If the Department of Finance had done its job of identifying loopholes in the tax system and found a mathematical formula that catches the abuse, then it is hard to argue that direct regulations or amendments could not be written that could equally well attack the abuse at lower compliance costs.
This confusing approach called "treatment by loan analogy" by finance officials has engendered fear within the leasing industry that the increasing administrative complexity it introduces will drive up costs.
On the other hand, companies that lease equipment fear that the disappearance of tax advantages for leasing as opposed to outright purchasing will constrain their cash flows. Both are problems, especially for smaller companies. The change of the date of implementation is designed to allow finance officials to implement the

change to lessors through either an additional amendment to the Income Tax Act or, preferably, to redraft the entire clause in a technical bill which they will introduce in either January or February.

She said: Mr. Speaker, the reason for this change is to nullify the effect of the gross up. The gross up of a quarter on income earned from dividends has the effect of driving up many seniors' incomes solely for the purpose of income tax calculation, if they earn part of their retirement income through dividends. This means that even if they do not earn $50,000 a year, the threshold for the clawback, they will be pushed over this mark and, as a result, have part or all of their old age security taxed back.
The grossup was originally introduced in order to avoid the double taxation of dividends. Dividends are taxed both at the corporate level and at the individual level. By including the gross up in his or her income tax calcula-
Govemment Orders
tions, the individual taxpayer receives a tax credit to avoid being taxed at the individual level. This is not a problem until the introduction of the clawback which has the effect that I have just described.

Mr. Speaker, I would just like to add to the words of our friend from Mission- Coquitlam. The whole concept of the gross up is to create some fictional income for purposes of income tax. The hon. member has correctly described what the reasoning behind it is. The idea was to avoid any perception of double taxation on dividends, and individual taxing on dividends would occur at a fairer level since some of those dividends had already had tax paid on them at the corporate level.
As the hon. member pointed out, what we have here is a situation where, assuming that the pensioner has retired with stocks which yield him or her something in the order of $40,000, with the 25 per cent gross up for reporting purposes that becomes $50,000, and suddenly the pensioner is in the position of losing the old age pension through the clawback. It was not real income, they still have the $40,000 to spend, but for a bookkeeping nicety they lose their pension income. That is the reasoning behind the proposed amendment. Once government members and backbenchers have a few moments to think about it, they will see that this particular clause ought to be deleted in the interest of fairness to pensioners.

Mr. Speaker, I have raised this matter of the dividend gross up a number of times in the context of questions to the minister in the House on the issue of the clawback. I am not sure that I agree with the amendment because I do not think it directs itself to the key issue. I think the amendment relating to the gross up in this context has to do with certain dividend rental arrangements that are provided for elsewhere in the amendments to the Income Tax Act contained in Bill C-28.
The point that my colleagues in the NDP are making with respect to the threshold and how it is calculated under the Income Tax Act for purposes of the clawback is an important one to make, that being that for the purposes of the clawback, which we will come to later on in the amendments, the threshold of $50,000 income is defined as income under Part I of the Income Tax Act.

December 15, 1989
And more than five members having risen:

That means that all dividends received from Canadian corporations will be grossed up by 25 per cent and that grossed up amount is the amount that is considered income for the purposes of the threshold of $50,000.
It has been pointed out by departmental officials that that is okay because to generate that many dividends, you have to have a lot of stocks, and that is true. But I would suggest that the essential inequity of treating different kinds of income differently for the purposes of the Income Tax Act undermines the integrity of the system. Whether we like the clawback or not, which clearly we on our side do not, if you are going to say that the threshold is $50,000 of income then let it be $50,000 of real income, not the notional gross up received on dividends.
Whether a senior puts his or her assets into interest earning investments or dividend earning investments should not make any difference in determining whether or not they have reached the threshold for clawback purposes. One of the most distressing things that has happened in this Chamber over the last 10 days is that the Minister of Finance in answering questions did not seem to understand what the dividend gross up was.
All of that being said, I do not think that this particular amendment addresses that problem. If there is going to be an amendment to address that problem, it needs to be done elsewhere in the act.

Mr. Speaker, the effect of this amendment is very simple. It is to delete the provisions of Bill C-28 that would introduce the clawback of old age pensions and family allowance benefits. I think it is fair to say that this one provision of Bill C-28 is the single most important social policy change in a generation in Canada. This, as the hon. member for Mississauga South, chairman of the finance committee has said, is the end of universality of social programs in Canada.
First, let me say that it is a disgrace this kind of social policy change is being made in the context of a budget bill so that there is no adequate opportunity for Canadians to debate this kind of change.

December 15, 1989
Government Orders
In January, 1985, that government issued a discussion paper under the name of the Minister of National Health and Welfare dealing with the universality of social programs and saying specifically that the clawback-it wasn't called that at the time-the idea of taxing back old age pensions, was unacceptable. It did suggest that maybe it was not so bad with family allowances, that is something we can debate, but it put it forward as a change in social policy that needed to be considered by Canadians, discussed and debated, in order to go forward with the evolution of social policy in Canada. That is the way it should have been done. It went to a parliamentary committee and nothing more was heard of it.
Then, in this year's budget, out comes the clawback as a fiscal measure. Yet it is changing a fundamental social policy in Canada. We could debate universality here, but we are not going to get very far in this forum on this kind of debate. Nor has there been an opportunity for the social agencies, for those groups representing the poor, those groups which are concerned with issues of social policy, to come forward and discuss this and give their input to it, given that it is put forward in a budget measure.
When you begin to change the principle of universality, the change goes far beyond affecting those few people who the government recognizes may be earning more than $50,000 a year at the present time. We believe that many of the programs that we offer, at all levels of government in Canada, should be made available equally to Canadians at whatever their income level. That has been true of the old age pension since 1952. That has been true of medicare. That has been true of education in the provincial jurisdiction. We say that Canadians should all receive the same basic social benefits, regardless of what their income is. That has been the principle. In abandoning that principle without full debate the government is doing a great disservice to Canadians across the country.
Government members will say, as the Minister has said, that this is not the end of universality. They think Canadians are so dumb that if they put money in one pocket and take it out the other, they will think they have been getting a universal benefit.
Let me put it to them this way. If this is not the end of universality, then what the government has introduced
with this measure is a discriminatory tax. It is a tax not based on ability to pay, as our other income taxes are supposed to be, it is a tax based on age or family size. No other groups in our society pay 100 per cent of any kind of income except, after this is fully implemented, those over 65 and have $50,000 of other income or those who are families.
I know I have very little time on this amendment. On old age pensions the fact is that Canadian pensioners paid for this pension. They paid with a special tax that was on their income tax forms from 1952 to 1971. If you go back to the debates in this Chamber in those years and read the words that were then spoken, it is clear the intention of the House of Commons was to ensure that all Canadians, regardless of their level of income, were entitled to the old age pension and that they were paying for it. When we changed the system in order to simplify it in 1971, Mr. Stanley Knowles rose at that time and expressed his concern that this was the beginning of the end of universality. Promises were made at that time that it was not going to be the end of universality. But here we are in 1989, and that is exactly what the government is doing.
What the government has forgotten on family allowances is the basic principle of fairness that should underlie the income tax system of horizontal equity; the fact that taxpayers who may have the same level of income carry different burdens on the part of our society. Taxpayers with families, with young children, contribute greatly to the future of Canada and that burden of doing so should be borne by all Canadians. This clawback measure does several things.
First, it puts families who have one income on a different footing from those who have two incomes. Two income families, in which both spouses earn $49,000 a year, do not face the clawback. A one income family, in which that one parent earns $60,000 a year, loses all of its family allowance. Is that fair?
The second thing is that years ago the government froze the child tax exemption and it changed it to credits. The government has whittled away the support for families and now, for many families, it has eliminated the family allowance benefit. It is clear that this government no longer believes that all Canadians have a stake in helping families with young children to contribute to the future. It has forgotten the basic principle of horizontal equity, if it ever understood it in the first place.
December 15, 1989

There is only one solution for this bill and that is to remove the discriminatory tax, the clawback tax, and send it into a discussion on social policy where it should have been in the first place so that all Canadians have an opportunity to present their concerns about it.

Mr. Speaker, I speak in support of the amendment proposed by my colleague, the hon. member for Ottawa South. I would just enunciate the danger that if this clawback tax is allowed to pass it will end the principle of universality in Canada.
I spoke earlier on this bill and I called it an attack on the very principle that has made the people of our country secure and which has been the cornerstone of our social policy.
This morning I would like, as a last attempt to change the heart of the government, to read from some of the thoughts of the very people who will be affected by this proposed tax by the government.
The National Council of Welfare, in its press release of September 13, 1989, said: "The elderly have already paid for their old age pensions through a lifetime of paying income taxes".
A letter from the President of the Senior Citizens Federation to Prime Minister Mulroney on June 23, 1989 stated: "We view this proposal as a serious breach of faith by our government and an insidious effort to undercut the social security programs that you have on numerous times stated are a sacred trust".
One Voice Canada indicated: "That penalizes people who receive benefits, specifically pensioners and families, and destroys the universal nature of the benefit."
The Coalition of Quebec Seniors, in a letter to Finance Minister Wilson on May 24 stated: "Your proposal creates a steeper tax rate for seniors than for others at similar income levels. Seniors who, with great difficulty, have succeeded over the years in saving for their retirement are being penalized".
The Coalition of Quebec Seniors in essence truly reflects the voice of seniors across the country. Not giving up the fight, in a letter addressed to most members of Parliament on November 29, 1989, they
Government Orders
again call to our attention that the implications of the clawback would be to reduce the purchasing power of seniors, to discriminate against them and to deal a death blow to the universality principle that we have so long cherished in Canada.
I would like to remind the government that the then hon. Minister for Health and Welfare, who is from my home province of Manitoba, promised on December 21, 1984, about this season of the year that: "All savings generated from any changes will be redistributed to social programs and will be applied to deficit reduction". And he continued: "The benefits from old age pensions will be taxed no differently from any other form of income".
That was a sacred promise of an hon. gentleman- whom I continue to esteem, a member of this government, a member of the cabinet in 1984-not so long ago, and this government today is doing just the opposite.
This government has broken a lot of promises and I submit that a litany of broken promises does not create a rosary of sacred trust. I am adamantly opposed to this clawback taxation of the pensions of the seniors of our country. I truly hope that in this spirit of Christmas there can be a change of heart, a change of mind and that the House will adopt the amendment proposed by my hon. colleague.

These are written comments of only a minute number of retired people within my community who have written to me as their member of Parliament. I am not the only one who has received hundreds of such letters. I am sure that everyone on the opposite side of the House has received hundreds of such letters as well but for some reason or other they have not got the courage to go against their Minister of Finance and vote out this clawback.

Mr. Speaker, I was concerned about some of the other clauses that we have been discussing this morning, but I am downright outraged about the proposed clawbacks of the old age security pension and the family allowance.
I have said before in this House, and I will say it again, that measures like the old age security and family allowance clawbacks are turning social policy into welfare policy and it is all being done in the name of harmonization.
My colleague, the member for Sault Ste. Marie, said that under the Prime Minister Canada's national vision has been replaced by a completely corporate vision. This government has sold off, shut down, privatized or cut back the best parts of that national vision. Air Canada, VIA Rail, Canada Post and CBC are only a few examples. Now, under this bill, the attack is on the most precious part of our national vision, universality of social programs.
Government Orders
Universal programs first attacked our old age security and family allowance. The question becomes what universal programs are going to be attacked second, third, fourth and fifth?
One of the members discussing this motion earlier talked about a CP wire story of 1984 which quoted the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister said: "Our position is simple and straightforward. We are in favour of universality in social programs and it shall not be touched". Has the Prime Minister lost touch? Has he lost control? Has he forgotten that promise?
I wanted to believe him during the last election campaign, as most Canadians wanted to believe him, that universality would not be touched. Seniors certainly wanted to believe him. But I submit to you, Sir, that actions speak louder than words. This legislation was introduced in a very secretive way, not through social policy as somebody earlier said, nor with any proper discussion in committees. It was in fact slipped through in this sort of catch-all of amendments in the hope that we would all forget and not notice. I suggest that this is not acceptable to Canadians.
Under the system of the finance minister, the income level at which the clawback starts will move upwards according to the same deindexing formula that exists in the tax system. In other words, a worker earning $40,000 a year and watching his or her income rise with inflation would be earning enough to put his or her income over the clawback level for family allowance of $56,309 by 1997.
For retirees the clawback is even more complex and phases in more slowly. But a simple rule of thumb is that a worker who earns his or her age, say a 28-year-old worker earning $28,000, or the average industrial wage today, will be hit by the clawback by the time he or she retires. This assumes that income keeps pace with inflation and that retirement income is 70 per cent of a pre-retirement income.
It follows that at $28,000 for a 28-year-old worker, $40,000 for a 40-year-old worker, $50,000 for a 50-year-old worker, within 20 years one in four Canadians will have all or part of their pensions clawed back. One million pensioners, within 20 years, will be caught in this clawback grab.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
speechtext:
If we got back to a balanced budget you wouldn't have to worry about it.

December 15, 1989

I am sure that the minister across the way who wants to interject will have an opportunity to speak to this too if he so wishes. The clawback will move our pension system closer to that of the U.S. where workers are covered by contributory pensions like RCPP and QPP or by means-tested programs like our Guaranteed Income Supplement, but not by a universal pension program like our Old Age Security. No pension exists in the United States, as a right of citizenship, for those over the age of 65.
It has been the finance minister's mission to shatter the universality barrier and once that principle is gone it will be a very simple matter to refine the clawback even further and make the programs more and more selective by taxing back higher and higher levels of benefits.
This clawback requires that some fundamental questions be asked. Why should an individual be entitled to receive $100,000 in capital gains, tax free, but lose the $4,000 he or she gets in Old Age Security simply because it was paid as a universal social benefit?

Mr. Speaker, Canadians and human rights activists around the world will mourn the passing of Mr. Andrei Sakharov. We will remember that more than 20 years ago Sakharov led that early fragile movement within the Soviet Union on behalf of human rights and international peace.
Sakharov was an individual who gave true meaning to the words of "courage" and "heart" and was concerned with his fellow men and women everywhere.
Sakharov, even in the last days of his existence, was challenging the present regime in the Soviet Union to move toward more progressive, open and democratic institutions. During his lifetime he challenged four separate Soviet institutions and in 1975 received the Nobel Peace Prize.
We mourn his passing. We recognize his great heart and his contribution to human rights world-wide.

Mr. Speaker, I too was deeply aggrieved to hear that Soviet human rights activist Andrei Sakharov died of a heart attack last night.
Mr. Sakharov, correctly called "the conscience of the Soviet Union", was recently elected to the Congress of the Peoples' Deputies and was working on constitutional reform of the Soviet political system when he died.
Mr. Sakharov in a real sense was a man of beautiful contrast. He built his eminence as a Soviet physicist who contributed to the development of the Soviet hydrogen bomb, but he did not allow that that tool of destruction should continue to be, for he later won a Nobel Peace Prize in 1975 for his advocacy of atomic disarmament, U.S.-Soviet co-operation in solving world problems and intellectual freedom in the U.S.S.R.
He was arrested in 1980 and sentenced to internal exile for his public opposition to Soviet foreign policies and for the Soviet government's suppression of dissidents and human rights activists. Later he was released. Despite personal persecution and exile, Mr. Sakharov worked tirelessly to promote the human rights issue in the Soviet Union and, indeed, the world over.
He will be remembered for his courage, his honourable principles and his selfless devotion toward peace. He died, but his mission to promote international respect for human rights as a guarantee of world peace will continue to live. We mourn his death. We are the beneficiaries of his mission.
December 15, 1989

Mr. Speaker, today the world mourns the passing of human rights activist and Nobel Peace Prize winner Andrei Sakharov.
Sakharov will go down in history as a man dedicated to peace and protection of individual liberties. As we watch the swirl of change in eastern Europe and the Soviet Union we often associate that change with the name Gorbachev, but for most of his adult life Andrei Sakharov was persecuted for promoting greater freedom and democracy for the Soviet people.
From his forced exile in Gorky, Sakharov was a beacon of hope for his compatriots and a symbol of dissent for peoples from around the world. He not only criticized the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan, but U.S. involvement in Vietnam, repression in the Middle East and racism in South Africa.
With his wife Yelena Bonner, Sakharov worked to change what was thought for so many years to be the unchangeable. Although we mourn the death of a great world figure and transmit our condolences to his wife and partner, Yelena Bonner, we take solace in the knowledge that Andrei Sakharov was able to see the fruits of his life work and long persecution.
The transformation of geopolitics we have experienced over the past months is a direct result of Andrei Sakharov. The world and our children's future are brighter for him.

Mr. Speaker, the minister of immigration recently responded to the forced deportation of Vietnamese refugees in Hong Kong by the British Government by criticizing their actions but did not offer any assistance on our behalf; nor did the minister show any international leadership to help the boat people who have been interned in refugee camps for years.
In fact the Canadian government's assistance to the Indo-Chinese over the next three years plans to accommodate only 16,000 people, which sadly pales in comparison to the 90,000 brought to Canada during the 1979-1980 period.
Conversely, under this government, the largest group of the wealthiest immigrants arriving in Canada under the immigrant investor program is from the same country in which the Vietnamese are presently being interned.
By refusing to assist the Indo-Chinese properly in their hour of need, the Minister of Immigration has set a course toward the rich and powerful. That is not only a dangerous course; it is also a colossal shame.

Mr. Speaker, despite record economic growth and the increasing prosperity of Canadians, NDP and Liberal members are busy perpetuating the myth that Canadians have been worse off since the Conservatives came to power. According to the statistics, the opposite is true. The number of Canadians living below the poverty line today is three-quarters of a million less than the figure recorded in 1984. Poverty levels have declined since 1984, from nearly 17 per cent to 13 per cent. The average family income has reached its highest level ever, with an increase of 1.8 per cent over 1987, after adjustment for inflation. Low income levels for children under 16 declined between 1984 and 1988 from 20.1 per cent to 15.4 per cent. The number of adult women-16 years of age or over-living below the poverty line dropped by 30,000 last year, adding up to a total decline of 229,000 since 1984. Poverty levels for senior citizens dropped between 1984 and 1988, from 21.6 per cent to 17.2 per cent. This is good news, Mr. Speaker! Our economic recovery program works. I think we should tell Canadians, and I hope the media will help us explain what is really happening in our society!

Mr. Speaker, on October 30 and again on December 6 constituents of Nepean and myself met in open fora to discuss the government's proposed GST. In addition, hundreds of letters have

December 15, 1989
been received in my office and, with the exception of a handful, all are opposed to the goods and services tax.
Nepean constituents are telling the government something very important. Despite the government's condemnation of people who dare to speak out against the GST and the assumption that they do not understand it, these people do indeed understand what the proposed GST is all about. They are vehemently opposed to it.
I find it appalling that this government seems not to care what the people are saying. I find it appalling that this government is ignoring the cries of millions of Canadians. I say these millions are right and the 167 members on the government side are wrong.
Canada is a democracy and Canadians are disillusioned and have lost faith because of the actions of this government. Canadians are saying: "Listen to us and drop this GST".

Mr. Speaker, the House should know that despite the rhetoric of several Conservative back-benchers, grain movement is proceeding normally off the prairies. Before freeze-up the Wheat Board always tries to empty Thunder Bay and leave lower St. Lawrence elevators full to meet sales commitments over winter.
Thunder Bay is still cleaning out. There are some 1.3 million tonnes of grain in stock; ample to fill the one ship loading, the two that are waiting and the six expected to arrive later in the week.
Lower St. Lawrence ports have plenty of grain to fill export demand. The flow to market has not changed.
There are problems within the seaway system with St. Lambert locks, as well as other operational problems, and recently the government has been unable to manage its labour relations. Back to work legislation only masks this point. Bill C-49 fails to live up to the government's own legislation on pay equity.
However, the bottom line is: the farmers' ability to deliver grain has not been affected. The Wheat Board has grain in position at the lower St. Lawrence in store and available for ocean ships. Thunder Bay will have space to receive prairie grain during the coming winter freeze-up.

Mr. Speaker, the Robert-Giffard Hospital near Quebec City is one of the most prestigious health care institutions in Canada. It is now conducting major research on psychiatric risk factors in children. This study is part of the Laval University-Robert Giffard Research Centre's clinical epidemiology program and follows a ten-year pilot study of child behaviour.
Mr. Speaker, today I wish to pay tribute to researchers at Robert Giffard Hospital who, under the supervision of Dr. Michel Maziade, an internationally known psychiatrist, are making an impressive contribution to the advancement of our medical knowledge of mental illness.
The people of Quebec and Canada owe a debt of gratitude to the Robert-Giffard Hospital for helping to improve the quality of life of the mentally ill and of society in general. I also wish to congratulate the Robert-Giffard Foundation which, together with the Government of Canada, provides financial support for this major research project.

Mr. Speaker, I want to draw the attention of the House to the deplorable condition of wharfs in my riding such as Graham's Pond, Georgetown and Launching, to name but a few.
If repairs are not done immediately, these wharfs will be washed into the sea by next spring. The harbour at Launching is well on its way. Part of the sea wall has given way and sands are filling the harbour.
At MacAulay's wharf the disrepair is threatening the environment. Diesel fuel tanks are sitting on a section of wharf that is sinking and diesel fuel is leaking into the harbour.

Once again I implore the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans to recognize the gravity of this situation, make Prince Edward Island fishermen a priority, and commit funds for the repair of wharfs today.

Mr. Speaker, two weeks ago we were all shocked and saddened by the senseless killing of 14 of the cream of our youth in Montreal.
I wish to draw to the attention of the House today that every day, 365 days of the year, we are killing 12 Canadians in traffic related accidents. In other words, over 4,000 Canadians lost their lives on our highways last year. At this time of year the carnage usually increases due to darkness, poor road conditions and increased alcohol consumption.
I call on all Canadians to use extra care in driving at all times, especially during the holiday season.
I call on all levels of government to pass and enforce whatever laws are necessary to reduce this terrible carnage on our highways.
I also make a special plea for support for research to help solve this escalating problem.

Mr. Speaker, for years the world has been concerned about the flagrant situation of human rights in Iran.
Reliable reports indicate that 90,000 political executions have taken place. The Peoples Organization of Iran has published a list of names and particulars of more than 16,000 of these victims which exemplifies the dimensions of human rights violations by the ruling regime in Iran.
While human rights violations continue unabated and news of mass executions in public are reported every day, international pressures and efforts of the Iranian Peoples National Resistance are taking place.
Those are the testimonies from the people who have escaped from the prisons and appeared before the United Nations special reporters. What is basically happening is violations of human rights according to the United Nations Charter which are unprecedented anywhere in the world.
S. ft 31
The Canadian government could offer its assistance to the special committee that will be going to Iran in a relatively few short weeks. The Canadian government could offer the help that is needed to substantiate all these charges against Iran and thereby call the regime in Iran to task to prevent such violations of basic human rights.

Mr. Speaker, the United Nations Children's Fund in its 1990 report on the state of the world's children spelled out that 38,000 children a day die and 100 million children in the next decade will die from hunger and its effects.
One must question the Canadian government's commitment to the 1.2 million Canadian children living in poverty when the Canadian government continually threatens to break our deficit over the backs of our children through measures like clawbacks on family allowance, reneging on child care, an ill-conceived 9 per cent tax grab, and threatened cut-backs on transfer payments under the Canada Assistance Plan.
The U.S. spends $1.5 million a day on military aid to El Salvador; twice as much as would be required to ensure that all of the children who die in the world each day would have been immunized and fed. Yet our federal government turns a blind eye.
What kind of credibility can Canada have at the UN on the matter of children's rights when the government is so negligent at home and abroad?

Mr. Speaker, today I would like to take this opportunity to pay tribute to Mrs. Marguerite Bernier, to whom I had the privilege of transmitting, on behalf of the Minister of National Health and Welfare, the Volunteer Canada Award's certificate of merit. The certificate is awarded annually to recognize and encourage the dedication of Canadian men and women who volunteer their time to improve the health and the quality of life of their fellow citizens.

December 15, 1989
Oral Questions
Mrs. Marguerite Bernier has been a dedicated fundraiser for the Eye Bank Foundation of Quebec, the Canadian Cancer Society, the Canadian Heart Foundation and the Multiple Sclerosis Society.
President of the Saint-CIaude-de-Laval senior citizens club since 1977, she has given her fellow members a new lease on life by organizing recreational activities and providing the help they need to have a better quality of life.
Mrs. Bernier, who will be 80 years old on March 3, 1990, is still an active member of the Laval-des-Rapides meals-on-wheels program and has been since 1982.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to respond to the comments made yesterday by the member for Sault Ste. Marie concerning the recent protocol amending the tax convention between Canada and Italy which addresses the taxation of certain pensions paid by the Italian state to residents of Canada.
At the outset I wish to indicate that the purpose of the new protocol was not to provide a fairer system of taxing pensions covered by the Canada-Italy Income Tax Convention.
Although the government believes that the protocol largely benefits Canadians in receipt of pensions from Italy, it should be pointed out that its purpose was not to secure a special or preferential status to a specific class of taxpayers but, rather, to ensure that the taxation of Canadian and Italian pensioners would be in accordance with Canadian tax policy.
An Italian pensioner with a small pension who is a resident of Canada receives the Guaranteed Income Supplement despite his level of other income.
To ensure that those in lower income brackets receive the exemption a threshold of $24,000 was provided. Residents earnings less than this amount receive their supplement free of tax; I repeat, free of tax.
For the majority of Canadian recipients Italy does not withhold tax. Where tax is withheld by Italy the Canadian resident can deduct the Italian tax from any Canadian tax
payable on their pension. There is no double taxation; I repeat, there is no double taxation.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to pose a question to the Minister of Finance.
Over the last several weeks this government has attempted to sugar coat the emerging economic crisis in this country. As the President of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association said yesterday, "there is clear evidence that we are slipping into a recession".
Is the Minister of Finance not alarmed by the fact that a Statistics Canada report points out that there will be 100,000 less jobs created this year than last year?
When is the Minister of Finance going to take his responsibilities seriously and correct the serious structural deficiencies the Prime Minister talked about yesterday?
When is he going to do something about the accelerating interest rates and the high exchange rates which are killing our exports?
When is the Minister going to start taking his responsibilities as the Minister of Finance and put some growth back in this economy, put some exports back in this economy, and do something about the people who are unemployed?

Mr. Speaker, I think if one looks at the record of this government and the ability and commitment of this government to deal with issues and to deal with problems as they come up, one can seriously understand why we are doing the things we are doing and why we have been successful over the last five years in having growth that is second only to the growth of Japan and just marginally behind the growth rate of Japan which is the fastest in the major industrialized countries.

The hon. member mentions structural problems. Are we dealing with structural problems? Yes, we are dealing with structural problems. One of the ways is the goods and services tax.
Oh, oh!
That's a problem all right.
Hon. members do not like me to mention this. The goods and services tax has been a major structural deterrent in the tax system for the last 50 years.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: It's going to be in future years is what you mean.

The hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier is giving me his advice.
Quite frankly, I will take the advice of the Organization of Economic Co-operation and Development and the International Monetary Fund, which organizations are saying that the importance of moving from the existing federal sales tax to the goods and services tax is a major structural change, a major initiative of this government. I intend to have something more to say about this with a statement in the House next Tuesday.

Mr. Speaker, I certainly agree with the minister that the proposed GST is a major structural problem. It is going to force up the inflation rate. It is going to force up interest rates. It is going to cause even more unemployment.
We now see the Canadian dollar at the highest rate in a decade. Interest rates are way beyond the historical average of 4.5 base points above American interest rates. Yet in his remarks yesterday the Governor of the Bank of Canada showed himself to be totally oblivious to the fact that the high interest rate policy is acting as a major deterrent to our exports, is having a crippling effect upon our regional economies, and is pushing this country into a recession.
When is the Minister of Finance going to assume his responsibility as the chief public policy maker in finance and to start setting guidelines that will bring interest rates down, bring the exchange rate down and start putting this economy back on track?
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, I think I have demonstrated over the last five years that I understand fully the importance of low interest rates. That was clearly a very important part of the strength of the economy during these past five years.
The hon. member says that the Governor of the Bank of Canada is oblivious to the problems. The person who is oblivious to these problems is the hon. member himself.
Let me quote from the report of the Organization of Economic Co-operation and Development which states: "Recent Canadian economic performance has been impressive and has brought the economy back to full capacity utilization". However, it noted that inflation and the budget deficit remain problematic and need to be addressed.
These are exactly the two issues that we are addressing. We addressed them in the 1989 budget. We are addressing them through monetary policy. We are going to continue to address them until we have these two problems solved.

Mr. Speaker, it is a tragedy that we have a Minister of Finance who prefers to listen to international bureaucrats and refuses to look at the reality in his own country.

Mr. Speaker, considering the latest alarming figures on Canada's international trade balance, will the Minister confirm that his government will not make any cutbacks in the export development program's budget? In other words, considering the major decline in our exports, would the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Trade not agree that any action to diminish the export development program would be disastrous?

Mr. Speaker, I delayed standing because I wanted to give my colleague, the Minister for International Trade, an opportunity to say what we are doing to promote international trade. I wanted him to talk about the broad program he has put in place which is supporting trade development both in Europe and the Far East as well as in the United States.

December 15, 1989
Oral Questions
These initiatives are all very carefully co-ordinated so that the Canadian exporting community will have good support from the Government of Canada in order to ensure that we are able to tap these markets and bring the jobs that will come from expanding international trade.
One key element of this is that we can have all the trade promotion in the world but if we do not have access to markets, then we do not get the trade coming back from it. The free trade agreement is so important to Canada in order for us to have access to the United States market and so that we do have the opportunities that will flow from that. That will come from the veiy aggressive trade promotion program my colleague has put in place.
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. To pretend that that free trade agreement has given us major enhanced access to the U.S. is a pot of nonsense.
Hear, hear!

To pretend that the record level of the Canadian dollar is enhancing our exports is again misleading the country.
Is the minister not going to recognize now the new economic realities? We are into a recession. Is he not going to alleviate and get away from this stubborn, bull-headed, pig-headed, one-way track of high interest rates?
Is he going to change his policy, which he is taking out on the backs of the unemployed, the farmers, the fishermen, the manufacturers and the exporters?

Mr. Speaker, that sort of excessive language is not going to make his points any better than the comments of his colleague from Winnipeg-
Let me just make reference to what the Pace University study on U.S.-Canada business had to say. It was announced just yesterday. It states: "The free trade agreement has had an extraordinary effect in stimulating the Canadian economy".
Hear, hear!

It is going to continue to have an extraordinary effect on ensuring that the
opportunities open to us in the United States economy will be there because of the free trade agreement.
The hon. member makes reference to monetary policy, as did his colleague in his earlier question. We understand the impact that this has on the economy, but we also understand that we have an inflation problem.
If the hon. member wants to look at the inflation statistics released just this morning, he will see that the inflation performance is still too high. We have to get this done because we know that far from having a temporary problem now with high interest rates we will have a long-term problem of lost productivity and lost competitive position. That will rob us of those opportunities in the United States on a long-term basis.
We learned some lessons in the 1970s. We on this side are not going to forget those lessons, not like the people on the other side of the House did. Clearly, they have forgotten the mess they got this country into in 1981.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, with a record high Canadian dollar we are effectively shutting ourselves out of that American market.
The minister, in addition to giving us the second highest interest rates of all major industrialized countries in the world is also, according to the Prime Minister's statement in the House last week, on another type of economic mission: it is to increase the record level of foreign investment in Canada. We already have the world's highest record of foreign control over our economy.
Let us look at the facts about foreign investment. Statistics Canada has shown over the last 10 years that we have brought in $1.2 billion through foreign investment. The outflow to those foreign investors over that 10-year period has been $128 billion. If for every one dollar of foreign investment that is brought in there is $107 that flows out, who is benefiting, Canada, or is it the foreign investors who are buying up Canada?
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member asks who benefits from investment. Canada benefits from investment by the jobs that are created and so on.

We applaud when GM expands its automobile plant in Oshawa. We applaud when Freightliner opens up a Greenfields plant in St. Thomas, Ontario. We applaud those investments.
Incidentally, Canadians are investing overseas in record amounts as well. However, over the last decade, in fact the percentage of foreign ownership in Canada has decreased, not increased.
The hon. member raises a valid question about foreign borrowings and the need to service that debt. He might ask the Government of Ontario about its extensive foreign borrowings, particularly the utilities. If you look at where the borrowings are occurring, it is more at the provincial level than at the federal level, particularly by Ontario and Quebec utilities.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Finance. I am not quite sure who he is, whether it is Mr. Crow or the member who is sitting there, but one of them can answer.
The government has created over one million fighters against inflation. There are over one million inflation fighters out there. The only problem is that they are all unemployed. I would like to know the minister's position on the following facts. According to the Canadian Exporters Association, every one cent increase in the value of the dollar costs us $1.3 billion in exports. In the lumber industry alone every one cent appreciation of the dollar costs us $100 million. This affects my province of British Columbia.
I would like to know when I go home and answer questions of people there who is running this show. Is it the minister or is it Mr. Crow? Who is responsible and who is making the decisions?

Mr. Speaker, it is a curious question the hon. member asked. They ask me that same type of question. They say: "Who is asking the questions, the member for Esquimalt or the President of the Canadian Labour Congress".
Oh, oh!

The simple answer to the question is that the government and the Governor of
Oral Questions
the Bank of Canada have extensive discussions on monetary policy. As a matter of fact, I had my regular weekly meeting with the Governor of the Bank of Canada just before coming to Question Period this morning. We have an ongoing relationship, an ongoing dialogue with the Governor of the Bank of Canada. We support the approach that the Governor is taking because we know the importance of getting the level of inflation down in order to avoid the problems that we got into as a country in 1981-82.
I remind the hon. member that the level of inflation was about 5.5 per cent in 1976. The government of the day forgot about that problem. It swept it under the carpet. Inflation started to creep up year after year. It reached a peak of 13 per cent in 1981. That led us directly into the huge mess that we got into with high interest rates of 20 and 25 per cent.
Every country did.

The hon. member says every country did. The hon. member should go back and check the numbers. She will see that the recession that we got into in Canada was far worse than that of the other industrialized countries.

Mr. Speaker, I am interested in hearing the minister respond by saying he met with Mr. Crow this morning and I am glad that he got his instructions from him. The instructions are what concern me.
Mr. Crow is suggesting that an unemployment rate of around 8 per cent is necessary to control inflation in Canada. Eight per cent will mean over 1.5 million unemployed in this country, all of whom will either have to go on unemployment insurance or social assistance.
Is it this government's policy to substitute a lower interest rate that would create jobs in this country by Canadians for Canadians? Is it the policy to substitute that for an increase in costs of welfare and unemployment insurance as a social and economic policy of welfare by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association and Mr. Crow?

Mr. Speaker, I understand the hon. member's frustration with high interest rates. I would like to get interest rates down as well. I know the difficulty of doing that in the face of the inflationary pressures in the economy today.

Oral Questions
The growth in business credit was at 11 or 11.5 per cent in recent months. The growth in household credit, while it has come down from about 18 per cent to 15 per cent, is still high. Those two levels of growth of bank credit at a time when the economy is growing at a nominal rate of 7 or 8 per cent is clearly inflationary.
The hon. member is suggesting that we jack up this growth in business credit, jack up this growth in household credit. What will that bring, Mr. Speaker? A great big bout of inflation and that is something we have to avoid in this country if we want to get back to the level of sustainable non-inflationary growth that we had in the last few years.

Mr. Speaker, it is a question of choices. The minister knows very well that by moving in the goods and services tax the government will move into the economy in a way that will draw more disposable income out of consumers' hands into the government's hands. That is number one. Number two, the minister knows very well that by keeping interest rates high the cost of borrowing by his government and previous Liberal governments continues to be high. That money is drained out of the economy as well. Therefore, you have to make choices.
The choice by this government is obvious. It would rather pay high interest charges, pay money out of general revenue to offshore borrowers and not create more wealth inside this country with manageable inflation figures. The choice is clear. I ask the minister: is it his decision, is it Mr. Crow's decision or is it the government's decision to keep paying high interest on borrowing and keep people unemployed in this country in order to serve some right wing mania?

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the question of the hon. member, but I ask him to reflect on his own record. When he came into office as Premier of the province of B.C., there was a hundred million dollar surplus. When he left, there was a hundred million dollar deficit. That is how much that hon. member knows about how he should run a government and run government policy.
The hon. member has said this is all about choices. Yes, it is about choices. There are very important choices
to be made here and we have made those choices. I think the record stands for itself over the last five years of what we have been able to do.
The hon. member has pointed out high interest rates and the effect that can have on the fiscal position of the Government of Canada as well as on the economy. We understand this. There has to be a reason why we have chosen this course of having a government fiscal policy and a monetary policy which is designed to get inflation down. That is because we understand what inflation will do to this country. We understand what that will do to interest rates on an ongoing basis and we understand how high inflation will damage the competitive position and the productivity of this economy on a long-term basis. This is what we are trying to stop. That is the choice we have made and I will stand by that choice.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Agriculture. Prairie farmers are facing the worst financial crisis in 50 years. In my province of Manitoba it is estimated that next year farm income will drop, not just a few percentage points, but a whopping 87 per cent. These are the minister's own figures. This is the man who has to be held accountable. This is the man who slashed farm support programs. My question is this: what is this minister going to do about this impending farm calamity?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just to set the record straight, between 1981 and 1984, when the Liberal party was in power, net realized farm income averaged $3.1 billion per year. In the last five years that average of realized net income has risen to over $4 billion, an increase of 30 per cent over the Liberal years. Therefore, Conservative years are certainly much better for the farmers of Canada than Liberal years.
In terms of direct assistance, between 1981 and 1984 under the Liberals some $500 million to $550 million in direct assistance was provided. Between 1985 and 1989 some $2.5 billion in direct assistance was provided. That is more than a fourfold increase.
December 15, 1989

We acknowledge that the projections for 1989 are not very good. It is a combination of low commodity prices, drought and a whole other host of factors. They are preliminary projections. We are as concerned as the hon. member. I appreciate him raising this. We are looking at it with the provinces. We are assessing it. As before, when the need is there, we will be there.

Mr. Speaker, I will tell you what the record is. The record is that 8,000 farmers in Saskatchewan are facing foreclosure. In that province food plants have closed and communities are dying. One person leaves Saskatchewan every 23 minutes. In the province of Saskatchewan, farm incomes are estimated to drop 100 per cent next year, worse than Manitoba. My question is this: how can this minister rip the guts out of farm support programs when farmers are losing their land and losing their livelihoods?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the Liberals were in office in 1984 there were some 550 bankruptcies occurring on the farm. That has dropped to around 200 in this year, which is still not good enough.
We have announced in the form of the Green Paper Growing Together the need for the establishment of new stabilization programs and safety nets. That is precisely what the agriculture conference this week was all about. That is a track that we are on, a program that we are proceeding with, in consultation with the provinces and with the producers.
As to whether there is a need for interim assistance, we are assessing that at the present time. As I have indicated before, the farmers know that this government has stood behind them in the past and it will stand with them again in the future.

Oral Questions
The minister will know that as a result of this particular decision, lobster fishermen in Atlantic Canada will lose $30 million a year for the next three years. Since we are not certain as to what sanction might be imposed under the free trade panel, which this issue has now been referred to, I ask the minister specifically whether he is prepared to provide today compensation for those fishermen in Atlantic Canada who are going to lose as a result of this negative decision by the President of the United States under the auspices of the free trade agreement.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International TVade):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the problem caused for the lobster fishermen of eastern Canada is a problem caused by the Congress of the United States, the Democratic majority leader in particular, Senator Mitchell, and the main delegation, who had Congress pass this particular law which the President signed for whatever his reasons were.
We have already taken steps to ensure that the matter is resolved as quickly as possible. We have asked the United States to expedite the free trade panel procedure so that we might have a decision at least a month earlier than would otherwise normally be the case. The estimate is that the damage to Canadian lobster fishermen could be in the area of $20 million to $30 million in a year. We hope to have the matter resolved in under a year.
With respect to the question of compensation, I am afraid this is not damage caused anyone by the Government of Canada. Therefore, there is no plan to give compensation to anyone in this connection.

Mr. Speaker, during the last election it was debated very vigorously by government members that we would have guaranteed access to the United States market. As a result of this decision by the American Congress, supported by the American President, that guarantee of access is no longer possible. This decision on the Atlantic fisheries is causing a major crisis, along with a lot of other issues in the fisheries.
I am fully aware of the representations that have been made and the fact that the minister is trying to expedite a decision under the free trade panel. We do not know what the sanction will be. As a measure of good faith, does the minister not think it appropriate, fair and just for him to place on the floor of the House of Commons an undertaking to Atlantic lobster fishermen to the effect that he will provide compensation up to $30

December 15, 1989
Oral Questions
million to those who are losing as a result of a regressive, negative attack on Canadian fishermen, particularly those in Atlantic Canada? Will the minister give us that undertaking?

Mr. Speaker, the rhetoric of the hon. member is certainly very impressive. I wonder if he could refer me to any precedent of a previous government, particularly our Liberal predecessors, where such compensation was arranged in any case similar to this.
No country has an alienable right to export its goods to any other country. Each receiving country decides what its domestic laws are and what laws that country will pass. We are taking steps under the GATT and under the free trade agreement, which is an improvement on the GATT, to have this action by the U.S. Congress and the administration reversed. If we are successful and the Congress does not reverse this legislation, we will proceed in accordance with international practice to impose a penalty on American exports to Canada. That is why the system works, and that is the way we will be pursuing this vigorously and I hope effectively.

My question is to the Minister of Finance. As the industry knows, the minister has had for the last two years the northern tax benefit which has benefited many Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Minister of Health. I made a statement earlier today in which I pointed out that over 4,000 Canadians have lost their lives on our highways in the last year. This amounts to 12 people every day who are killed on our highways. It is particularly true at this time of year. In the statement I implored all levels of government to do whatever they can to improve this record.
I ask the Minister of Health today just what the federal government is doing to reduce this carnage on our highways.
Hon. Perrin Beatty (Minister of National Health and
Welfare): Mr. Speaker, the hon. member's question is particularly timely at this time of year when issues related to impaired driving are particularly important.
Today my department is releasing a major survey as to Canadian's attitudes and practices in drinking and driving. One of the things that it shows is that in the year that preceded the survey, two and one half million Canadians had driven with a driver whom they felt was impaired, whom they felt had had too much to drink.

The problem is particularly acute among young Canadians between the ages of 16 and 24 who represent only a small part of the total population. My question basically is based on the fact that we have an undue amount of violence, alcoholism, drug abuse and suicide. Will the government now admit that the programs it has in place do not work? speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:

In addition, we believe strongly that a program of transferring responsibility for health services on reserves to the native populations allows local control in terms of planning and delivery of health services. We believe that something is vital.
There have been many examples, most strikingly in the Hobbema reserve outside of Edmonton, where there has been dramatic progress by the local community working to bring down, first, the suicide rate and, second, to dramatically bring down the rate of problems related to drinking and to drug abuse. It is an example of how things can be done. The department continues to work closely with native groups in terms of assisting them.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary is to the Minister of Justice. The horrible social conditions faced by aboriginal peoples is borne out over and over again in evidence brought before several judicial inquiries.
There have been many calls for a native justice system. Will the minister inform this House when the government will take steps to establish such a system?

As you know, the American judiciary is still detaining trucker Richard Bilodeau, and there seems to be a great deal of confusion here in Ottawa about the extradition treaty.

Americans that manslaughter is an extraditable offence under the legislation. Everything possible has been done to assist this unfortunate Canadian citizen, Mr. Bilodeau.

He has made it within the last few days. I know that the minister, as a lawyer and a minister of the Crown, is very concerned about due and proper process. On page 2 of the conflict of interest guidelines it states:

Did Mr. Jarvis sign the certification as required and if so, why did he continue to serve when he was in violation?

In this instance Mr. Jarvis has confirmed that he was certainly well aware of those guidelines and that he would comply with them. In fact, as a member of the board of directors which approved the guidelines, he obviously was aware of them and now has complied with the requirements as indicated.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs or in his absence, the acting secretary of state, with respect to the very rapidly deteriorating situation in the northern part of Ethiopia, the resumed threat of famine to as many as 5 million people, the increasing civil conflict that prevents many of those people from being reached under the present circumstances.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International Trade):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member who just asked that question of course has had extensive experience in Ethiopia and I know his concern is very genuine. We have been working with other donors. We have been working with UN organizations and international relief agencies to persuade the Government of Ethiopia to allow access to those who are starving in northern Ethiopia. We were encouraging the UN organizations to ensure that a co-ordinator, either in New York or Addis Ababa as was the case in 1984 and 1988, act as a focal point for the relief organizations and strive to win co-operation of the parties in Ethiopia.
Finally, the government has approved $17.7 million in food aid and emergency relief assistance to Ethiopia this year: $13.4 million to the Canadian non-governmental organizations and $4.25 million to the World Food Program and UNICEF.

His report is being reviewed urgently to try to ensure that we have in place a mechanism which is adequate to meet the challenge. This is being given every attention and priority.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (President of the Treasury Board):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a result of the government's expenditure review process, I am in a position today to announce a package of initiatives designed to make government operations more efficient and to save Canadian taxpayers $1.4 billion over the next three years.
These actions are the latest step in our constant efforts since 1984 to manage frugally. They follow the hard decisions announced last spring in the budget.
I would like to underline that the Minister of Finance and I will be announcing further reductions in spending in the new year. The government is continuing to review expenditures in order to adhere to our fiscal plan as we prepare early in the new year for the next budget and the Main Estimates.
When Canadians used to look at the federal government operations they would see red: red tape and red ink. The measures I am announcing today will help us make solid progress on both.

Mr. Speaker, the very real success we have had in bringing government spending under control is sometimes overlooked. Since 1984, we have taken a number of steps, often difficult and sometimes unpopular, to eliminate wasteful practices and spending by introducing a more businesslike approach to the operations of government. These have included expenditure and program reviews, reductions in payments to and privatization of Crown corporations, reductions in the size of the Public Service and cost-recovery measures.
As a result of these measures, we have kept annual growth in program expenditures to 3.6 per cent, well below the inflation rate. Compare that, Mr. Speaker, to the annual 14.1 per cent growth which occurred during the last five years of the Liberal administration.
Routine proceedings
We have met our objective of reducing the size of the Public Service. It is now the size it was 17 years ago, and that in spite of a heavier workload.

We have improved cash management. This alone has saved taxpayers nearly $1 billion since 1985. We have been leading the country in terms of leadership vis-a-vis wage settlements.
In the last round we have averaged an increase of 4.2 per cent per year for the total of the federal Public Service. We have reduced program spending to the point where we expect budgetary revenues to exceed programs spending by about $9 billion this year. That is a very significant improvement. We inherited on coming into office a $12 billion deficit in program spending, and we now have a $9 billion surplus.
This government has done more to control spending and to improve programs and services than any other government in recent history. We know that Canadians have not found it easy to accept many of the restraint measures that were necessary to manage the economy and ensure our future. I want Canadians to know that the government has been tightening its belt and will continue to do so.
Today's package is real. It is difficult. In fact it will not only mean doing better and more with less; in some cases it will mean doing without. However that is what leadership is all about and there is no better place to start than right here in this great institution.
This week the Board of Internal Economy which oversees the expenditures of the House of Commons reached an all-party agreement on a number of measures which will save Canadian taxpayers several million dollars. First of all we will save half a million dollars by cutting grants to parliamentary associations and by cutting budgets for foreign travels and visits by parliamentarians by 20 per cent.
We will save up to $730,000 by closing two parliamentary cafeterias and a private dining room and lounge for members of parliament, as well as reducing cafeteria operating hours. We will be raising prices to increase cost recovery from the parliamentary dining room and catering services.

December 15, 1989
Routine proceedings
We will save $300,000 by implementing a two-year freeze on certain aspects of members' non-salary budgets.

We will terminate a broadcasting studio service to Members of Parliament for an immediate saving of $300,000 and we will save over $1 million through a 20 per cent reduction in the cost of pamphlets which Members send to their constituents.
Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate Members of all parties on the Board of Internal Economy for deciding to take these measures because they have shown their willingness to provide leadership during a period of fiscal restraint. In so doing, we, as Parliamentarians, are setting an example in our own house.
That is why the govemmeent will reduce the budget of the National Capital Commission by $8 million a year. It will also defer expenditures on projects such as underground parking and statues on Parliament Hill.
Furthermore, we will reduce spending on Confederation Boulevard and official residences. Specifically, renovation of 7 Rideau Gate, the government's guest house, will not proceed. This alone will make it possible to save $3 million over the next three years.
Other major capital projects, totalling $3 million, at Rideau Hall, 24 Sussex and Harrington Lake are also being deferred.

We have ordered an immediate 20 per cent reduction in international travel by public servants.
In addition, we will sell two of the eight Challenger jets used by the government for ministerial travel. One reason we can do without the two Challenger jets is that ministerial travel has decreased very significantly since 1983-1984. The average number of flying hours per month has dropped by 25 per cent. The average number of flights per month has decreased by 37 per cent.
There is much more that we as a government will do to make major savings of taxpayers' dollars and make those dollars work harder and better. We have decided to extend by two years the two per cent cap on increases to the operating and maintenance budgets of government departments.
This 2 per cent ceiling has been in effect for the past four years and was due to expire. Extending the ceiling two more years will challenge managers in the Public Service to do better with less. In some cases it will lead to trimming in some programs and services. This measure, which is the largest single saving in the package, will require ongoing restraint in government departments and will realize roughly $450 million a year.
We have ordered a two-year freeze on construction projects worth some $460 million planned for the national capital region. Only those projects required for safety or health reasons or to maintain essential operations will be allowed to proceed with construction during this period. This will save $70 million over the two-year period.
We will reduce the operating budget of External Affairs by $70 million over the next four years. In addition, we will cut Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation's administration and research budget by $3 million.

We will introduce a "blue box" paper recycling program and related measures which will improve the environment and save more than $1 million a year.
The government will also be taking a series of cost-recovery initiatives, totalling $390 million over three years. This reflects a new policy which gives departments the opportunity to retain a portion of cost-recovered revenue. The following initatives will be taken: we will increase fees for processing immigration and visitor visa applications and for entering and using national parks; we will add new administrative fees for processing student loans and improve the collection of overdue payments on those loans; and we will eliminate the $175 million annual subsidy to the Post Office and replace it with a better-targeted program of direct support to Canadian publishers. Part of the savings will be redirected to other programs of the Department of Communications.
Hear, hear!

As I said earlier, these cost-saving measures will challenge managers in the Public Service to do better with less. A supporting component of today's package, therefore, is an important set of measures to improve the management and delivery of government programs and services. This includes incentives for more effective program and budget management, as well as the restructuring of several government agencies and organizations. A major innovation will be to allow Public
December 15, 1989

Service managers to carry over three per cent of non-salary operating and maintenance funds into the following fiscal year. This should allow wiser spending by putting an end to the pressure on managers to use funds at the end of the fiscal year just to avoid losing them.

We are also introducing an innovative concept of management in government called special operating agencies. These agencies are pilot projects to improve the delivery and cost efficiency of services offered by the government. They will operate within government in a business-like manner with flexibility that is necessary to achieve agreed upon bottom line results.
Some of these agencies will compete with the private sector as suppliers of services to the government and will have to give account for the results at the end of each year. We will convert the passport office, the government telecommunications agency and the Public Service Commission staff training program into special operating agencies. As a result they will have multi-year business plans and specific business goals.
We are merging the publishing and printing operations of Supply and Services Canada and the mapping service of Energy, Mines and Resources Canada. They will then become one special operating agency.
Two other divisions of Supply and Services-the Audit Services Bureau and the Bureau of Management Consulting-will also be consolidated and converted into one special operating agency.
We are closing down the government's exhibit production facility and the Canadian government photo centre.
We will use computer based systems to improve asset management. We will provide incentives to managers to dispose of surplus assets and to increase fees for service by allowing departments to retain a portion of the proceeds for reinvestment to improve the services that generate the revenue.
Routine proceedings
We will contract out the operations of the Canada Student Loans Program and increase contracting for translation services.

Mr. Speaker, these are all substancial measures. As I said earlier, they are designed to cut red tape and red ink.
Canadians have demanded that the government improve its performance and budget management. We have heard them loud and clear.
As the Prime Minister said recently when he announced the Public Service 2000 Program, it is essential that the Public Service be modernized to meet changing conditions and to provide better services.
He also rightly pointed out that the Public Service has to be improved as an institution that can offer careers to people devoted to serving their fellow citizens.
Mr. Speaker, the measures I have announced today are substantial, but more has to be done. That is why I say that today's announcement is part of an on-going process.
Mr. Speaker, this government is committed to more than the bottom line. It is committed, in a thoughtful and on-going way, to providing Canadians the quality of service and the quality of life which they so richly deserve.
I had the pleasure to table, in both official languages, detailed information on the package I have just announced.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to respond this afternoon to the statement made by the President of the Treasury Board who henceforth will be renamed Ebenezer Bob. Ebenezer Bob has perpetrated the announcement this afternoon on Canadians just before the Christmas season.
In large measure this statement is a smoke screen announcement. It is to hide the real biggy which will happen next Tuesday, as admitted by the Minister of Finance a little earlier this morning in response to a question by one of my colleagues.

December 15, 1989
Routine proceedings
Next Tuesday, I predict, the Minister of Finance will be announcing the biggy to which I referred previously. It will be a sledgehammer on Canadians, his much dreaded GST which is known as the goods and services tax or perhaps more appropriately the grief and suffering tax.
The GST the minister will announce in a few days at whatever rate will be unacceptable to Canadians. The measures announced today will not camouflage or hide the fact that Canadians are displeased with what the government is proposing.

Mr. Speaker, there are in fact three main components in today's government statement. For openers, there is a reference to cut-backs in parliamentary services. I will get back to this point later on, but for now I want to point out that when services are reduced the immediate victims are always the people who are on the lowest rung of the salary scale.
